extracted.intended_audience: healthcare providers, health insurers/issuers, plan sponsors, third-party administrators, pharmacies, legal counsel, and other covered entities implementing or evaluating compliance with Section 1557 nondiscrimination requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards governing how Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act applies to health programs and activities (including health insurers, benefit plans, TPAs, pharmacies, and providers), what entities and products are covered or excluded, and how nondiscrimination and accessibility requirements should be applied in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on benefit limits that discriminate
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must not impose limitations on the frequency or number of benefits (for example, limiting therapy visits to once per week or limiting prescription drug coverage to a 30-day supply) that have discriminatory effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include arbitrary caps on therapy visit frequency or limiting drug supplies; such limits can function as discriminatory barriers to care and are subject to scrutiny under Section 1557. (Context: opening line of chunk.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with ADA accessibility requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities are required to comply with accessibility requirements in the Americans with Disabilities Act (see 45 CFR 92.303 and other ADA-related provisions incorporated into Section 1557 obligations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule cites 45 CFR 92.303 (section 1557) and notes covered entities must meet certain accessibility requirements in the ADA; OCR will look to ADA standards when assessing accessibility obligations under Section 1557.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer employment-practices exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule does not apply to employers with regard to their employment practices, including the provision of employee health benefits (per § 92.2(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although employee health benefits may be discussed elsewhere, the text explicitly states the rule does not apply to employers' employment practices, clarifying a carve-out from coverage for those employer activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-term limited duration insurance (STLDI) exclusion and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-term limited duration insurance is generally exempt from title XXVII PHS Act consumer protections and is excluded from the definition of ‘individual health insurance coverage’; currently defined as coverage effective for less than 12 months (and up to 36 months accounting for renewals), with a proposed revision to narrow initial contract period to no more than 3 months and total duration no more than 4 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Departments note STLDI is defined by HHS, Labor, and Treasury; the NPRM proposed narrowing the definition (88 FR 44596 (July 12, 2023)); because STLDI is excluded from certain PHS Act requirements, it affects which nondiscrimination protections apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandfathered plan limitations and maintenance of status
rubrics_metrics.description: Grandfathered health plans (plans in effect as of ACA enactment) remain subject only to certain market reforms and are not subject to some nondiscrimination reforms; to retain grandfathered status, plans cannot make certain changes to benefits, cost-sharing, or contribution rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains the statutory basis for grandfathered plans (42 U.S.C. 18011; 45 CFR 147.140) and that certain changes will cause loss of grandfathered status, which affects the application of nondiscrimination and other ACA consumer protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grandmothered plans and conditional non-enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain non-grandfathered health insurance coverage in the individual and small group market (‘grandmothered’ plans) may be treated as not out of compliance with specified market reforms under certain conditions, including those related to nondiscrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to CMS extended non-enforcement policies explain that some plans may be temporarily treated as compliant under limited circumstances; this affects enforcement of nondiscrimination-related market reforms for such plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: health insurers and issuers receiving federal assistance are covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Entities such as health insurance issuers, including Medicare Advantage organizations and Part D plan sponsors that accept federal assistance or contract with CMS, can fall within the definition of a ‘health program or activity’ covered by Section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations and case law (e.g., Fain v. Crouch; Doe One v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc.) are used to support that insurers and issuers accepting federal funds or contracting with federal programs may be required to comply across their portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party administrator (TPA) and subsidiary liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party administrators and interrelated entities can be liable under Section 1557 for discriminatory plan terms when the discriminatory provisions originated with them or they designed and provided discriminatory provisions to plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule references case law (Tovar v. Essentia Health; C. P. by & through Pritchard v. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Ill.) holding TPAs may be liable even where employers adopted plans, and gives guidance that OCR will analyze subsidiary liability and application to TPAs.

rubrics_metrics.name: ERISA does not supersede Section 1557 nondiscrimination obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: ERISA requirements (including fiduciary duties and the duty to administer plans as written) do not alter or exempt entities from Section 1557 nondiscrimination obligations; Section 1557 is dominant where there is a conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 29 U.S.C. 1144(d) and case law (e.g., C. P. by & through Pritchard; Tovar) indicating courts will not construe ERISA to impair Section 1557; fiduciaries must act consistent with nondiscrimination obligations despite plan documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiduciary duties must be exercised consistent with nondiscrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan fiduciaries' statutory duties (see 29 U.S.C. 1104(a)(1)(D)) to act solely in the interest of participants and in accordance with plan documents are constrained by Section 1557's nondiscrimination mandate when documents conflict with nondiscrimination obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule highlights that administering a plan 'as written' is subservient to Section 1557 and fiduciaries cannot rely on plan documents to justify discriminatory terms; courts have applied this principle in relevant cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network adequacy and geographic/service-area considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of network limitations should consider factors such as geographic location of the service area, number of available providers and specialists, reimbursement rates, number of providers willing to contract, and the overall plan design as it relates to premiums; virtual care and medical travel may reduce geographic limitations where clinically appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text quotes prior discussion (87 FR 47877) enumerating these factors and notes industry changes (growth in virtual care) that may affect the weight given to geographic limitations when assessing discriminatory access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible equipment and interior elements requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered health care facilities should have accessible medical equipment and interior elements to meet the needs of people with mobility disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References National Council on Disability and empirical studies (e.g., Mudrick et al.) supporting the necessity of accessible equipment; the final rule's requirements do not preclude other federal eligibility rules but stress accessibility as an enforceable expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmacies' obligation to ensure nondiscriminatory access
rubrics_metrics.description: Retail pharmacies have obligations under federal civil rights laws to ensure nondiscriminatory access to health care at pharmacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agencies reference HHS guidance to retail pharmacies (Sept. 29, 2023); the guidance clarifies it does not require pharmacies to fill prescriptions in violation of state law (e.g., state abortion restrictions). OCR enforcement and guidance may be relevant to pharmacy practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on associational discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrimination on the basis of association with a protected person or class (e.g., being forced to provide an interpreter because of a parent's disability) is prohibited under the incorporated civil rights statutes and Section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule cites case law (Falls v. Prince George's Hosp. Ctr.; Holcomb v. Iona Coll.; Larimer v. IBM; and many others) demonstrating recognition of associational discrimination across statutes (ADA, Title VII, Title IX, Section 504). Associational claims are actionable under these frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entities principally engaged in health care may be covered across operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have found that entities 'principally engaged in the business of health care' can be covered by Section 1557 across their operations, including separate business lines (e.g., pharmacy benefit managers or pharmacy chains), where the interrelationship among entities renders them functionally part of the health program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doe One v. CVS Pharmacy, Inc. is cited as an example where the court concluded CVS and interrelated entities were covered; the agencies caution against letting form obscure substantive interrelationships that would undermine enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with other federal laws and parallel regulatory citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the rule cites HHS regulations, other Departments (Labor, Treasury) have parallel statutory and regulatory authorities; interactions with other federal laws (e.g., Medicaid/Medicare statutes, ERISA, PHS Act provisions) affect interpretation and application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule often cites HHS regulatory sections while noting parallel citations in Labor and Treasury; practitioners should consult parallel authorities where relevant (e.g., definitions of excepted benefits, short-term insurance, and applicability to specific programs).
